UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY
FINANCIAL CRIMES ENFORCEMENT NETWORK
IN THE MATTER OF No. 2001 - 02
ANGELINA PLETT
ASSESSMENT OF CIVIL MONEY PENALTIES
AGAINST ANGELINA PLETT
I. INTRODUCTION
The Secretary of the United States Department of the Treasury has delegated to
the Director of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (“FinCEN”) the authority to
determine whether a financial institution has violated the Bank Secrecy Act, 31 U.S.C.
§§5311 et seq. and 31 CFR Part 103 thereunder (“BSA”), and what, if any, sanction is
appropriate.
II. JURISDICTION
Angelina Plett (“Plett”) was, at all relevant times, an owner and the manager of
Cash For Checks Inc. (“Cash For Checks”). Cash For Checks was, at all relevant times, a
licensed check casher located in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma and was a “financial
institution” within the meaning of 31 U.S.C. §5312(a)(2) and 31 CFR §103.11(n).1
III. FINCEN’S DETERMINATIONS
A. Structuring
FinCEN has determined that between July 11, 1995, and April 26, 1996, Plett
willfully structured or willfully assisted in structuring check cashing transactions for
Joseph A. Sivigliano (“Sivigliano”) through a domestic financial institution in violation
of 31 U.S.C. §5324(a)(3) and 31 CFR §103.63(c). During the relevant time period,
Sivigliano cashed 136 checks totaling more than $1.17 million at Cash For Checks. On
each of 43 days, Sivigliano cashed a series of checks that individually totaled less than
$10,000, but that together exceeded $10,0

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5324?
statutory.answer: Neutral — the facts suggest possible structuring, but they do not establish the required intent to evade reporting; 31 U.S.C. § 5324 prohibits structuring to evade reporting requirements.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5324 applies when a person (i) structures or attempts to structure a transaction (or causes/attempts to cause a financial institution to fail to file a required report) (ii) for the purpose of evading a reporting requirement under the Bank Secrecy Act (e.g., CTR reporting for currency transactions over $10,000). Here, the fact pattern shows multiple inbound deposits—many in cash—generally below $10,000 (e.g., $7,357.14; $4,124.65; $7,163.36; $7,938.59; $8,822.45) over several days and from multiple counterparties, with notes labeling them “smurfing fan-in deposit,” which is consistent with the actus reus of breaking up cash deposits. However, § 5324’s key mens rea element is purpose/intent to evade a reporting requirement; the facts do not state that any single day’s cash deposits were aggregated at one financial institution in a way that would otherwise trigger a CTR, nor do they provide evidence of intent (e.g., statements, instructions to keep deposits under $10,000, prior CTR history, bank interactions, or knowledge of reporting rules). The presence of ACH credits (not CTR-triggering) further leaves ambiguity about whether the pattern was designed to evade currency reporting versus ordinary business receipts. Therefore, while the pattern is suspicious, the record is insufficient to conclude the conduct falls within § 5324; 31 U.S.C. § 5324 prohibits structuring to evade reporting requirements.
